Inferred spatial localization of neuronal subtypes. Visium spots are colored by the predicted proportion of each indicated subtype, mapping transcriptional changes to anatomical space.

a, Dot plots showing maximum and mean log-normalized expression of neuropeptide genes and receptors across all hypothalamic neurons (213,469 nuclei from all young, CTL, AD and AD_44 donors). Error bars in mean-expression plots show the standard deviation across nuclei. This panel is descriptive. b, Concordance of AD-associated log2 fold changes between HypoAD (x-axis) and PsychAD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (y-axis) in GABAergic (left) and glutamatergic (right) neurons. Each point represents a gene significant in both datasets (FDR < 0.05). For each gene and lineage, the result with the lowest FDR across constituent neuronal subtypes was selected. HypoAD differential expression used one pseudobulk per sample (AD versus CTL, edgeR likelihood-ratio tests), whereas PsychAD used one pseudobulk per donor. Two-sided, unadjusted Spearman correlations: GABAergic ρ = 0.028, n = 765 genes, P = 0.45. Glutamatergic ρ = 0.296, n = 301 genes, P = 1.7 × 10−7. Genes are correlation units, not biological replicates. Black and pink indicate concordant and discordant directions, respectively. Dashed lines indicate zero.

a, Ranked bar charts of univariate AUROC for distinguishing AD status using neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores (top) and MRI-derived volumetric measures (bottom). MRI participant counts are as in b. b, Cross-modal comparison of univariate AUROC between MRI-derived volume and neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores for matched hypothalamic regions (1:1 pairing). Left: snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC, with a dashed line indicating equal performance. Right: AUROC estimates for each modality by region, with lines connecting matched estimates. Each dot represents one AUROC estimate, not a biological replicate. No error bars or cross-modal tests are shown. Score direction was chosen so that AUROC ≥ 0.5. The dashed vertical line indicates chance (AUROC = 0.5). MRI AUROCs used 316 participants: 24 with AD, defined as cognitively impaired and amyloid-β positive, and 292 without AD. snRNA-seq AUROCs used donor-level pseudobulks from 14 biologically independent donors (7 AD, 7 control) for ARC, PVH, SCN, MN, PO, TM, ZI and the whole hypothalamus, 13 donors (7 AD, 6 control) for LH, and 10 donors (5 AD, 5 control) for VMH and DMH. c, Cross-modal comparison as in b, with snRNA-seq AUROC averaged across neuronal subregion annotations containing the matched region. For example, AN includes ARC, ARC_SCN, ARC_SMN, LH_ARC, PO_ARC, SCN_ARC, VMH_ARC and ZI_ARC. Left: mean snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC. Right: bars show MRI AUROC and mean snRNA-seq AUROC, and dots show individual annotation AUROCs. Error bars show sample standard deviations (n − 1 denominator) across annotations and appear only when at least three annotations match. Matching annotation counts are 8 (AN/ARC), 6 (Pa/PVH), 4 (VM/VMH), 10 (SCN), 2 (DM/DMH), 4 (MM/MN), 7 (MPO/PO), 1 (TM), 5 (ZI), 3 (LH) and 1 (whole hypothalamus). Standard deviations describe variation across annotations, not donor-level uncertainty. No inferential comparison was performed. All annotations originate from the same pool of 14 donors (7 AD, 7 control), so AUROCs averaged within a region are not statistically independent. MRI AUROCs and participant counts are as in b. AN and DM denote the arcuate nucleus and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (ARC and DMH in the main text).

a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Fresh whole hypothalamus was obtained from eight 8-month-old female mice: four wild-type (WT) and four 5xFAD heterozygous (HET). Tissue underwent Dounce homogenization, debris cleanup and nuclei isolation. Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Chromium Controller, and 3′ gene-expression libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq platform, yielding 60,479 nuclei for analysis. b, UMAP of 60,479 nuclei, colored by major cell type: astrocytes, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, microglia, leukocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, OPCs and fibroblasts. c, Cross-species cell-type correspondence. Heatmap of Spearman correlations between human HypoAD cell types (columns) and mouse 5xFAD cell types (rows), with mouse cell types labeled using transferred human annotations. High diagonal values indicate concordant cell-type identities across species. d, Microglial expression of homeostatic (Csf1r, Cx3cr1, P2ry12), DAM1 (Apoe, B2m, Ctsb) and DAM2 (Axl, Itgax, Timp2) markers in four WT mice (465 nuclei) and four HET mice (912 nuclei). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Arrows indicate the direction of change in HET. Genotype effects were estimated using linear mixed models of per-nucleus expression (genotype fixed effect, random intercept for mouse, lmerTest). Two-sided t-tests used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, with Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment across nine genes. Genotype coefficients (HET − WT, 95% confidence interval) and adjusted P: Csf1r −0.36 (−0.73 to 0.01), 0.073. Cx3cr1 −0.33 (−0.60 to −0.06), 0.037. P2ry12 −0.37 (−0.65 to −0.09), 0.037. Apoe 0.62 (0.44 to 0.80), 1.3 × 10−4. B2m 0.06 (−0.08 to 0.21), 0.36. Ctsb 0.25 (0.06 to 0.43), 0.037. Axl 0.09 (0.03 to 0.16), 0.037. Itgax 0.06 (0.01 to 0.11), 0.037. Timp2 0.08 (−0.12 to 0.28), 0.37. ns, nonsignificant, *adjusted P < 0.05, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Each point represents one gene. Representative genes are labeled. f, Selected significantly enriched Hallmark pathways from GSEA of the 5xFAD-versus-WT comparison in astrocytes, neurons and oligodendrocytes. Fill color indicates the normalized enrichment score (NES). Gray indicates pathways not significantly enriched in that cell type. #1411. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

Jaydee Canvot glances the ball into his own net and Brighton lead! 🔵 https://t.co/subm9ggwId

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. And so, just as he entered the centre circle in the opposition half, Gómez attempted the absurd.

"Would you look at that!" DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 https://t.co/qmagVbGEb4

“I’m not training with Diego Gómez shooting from 50 metres in training,” head coach Fabian Hürzeler said while breaking into a smile. “It’s just about making the players quick in their minds.

“In these moments it’s about being very precise with his long kick. The perception to recognise the keeper and being quick to go to the action was impressive.”

The presence of mind to attempt something outlandish was one thing; the execution was quite another. With Benítez vulnerable, Gómez took just one touch with his right foot before taking his shot, not giving the keeper enough time to scramble back to cover his line. As he looked up to confirm the opportunity, the 23-year-old struck the ball over Benítez with such venom that it did not even bounce until it reached the goal.

All that remained was for the Paraguayan international to hurtle towards the corner flag, engulfed by his ecstatic team-mates. For the Brighton fans, soaked by showers at the Amex, rain can never have felt so sweet.

Gómez’s goal will earn comparisons with David Beckham’s lob from the halfway line at Wimbledon. The advancements in pressing and conditioning in the 30 years since, with space ever more congested, makes such a strike even harder today. Not since Wayne Rooney in 2017 has a player scored a Premier League goal from further out than Gómez’s 56 yards.

Gómez may well attempt an encore. He shot from even further out at the Stadium of Light a week ago. When October ends, three of the last four Premier League goal-of-the-month winners will be Brighton players. Alongside his meticulous emphasis on set-pieces, Hürzeler empowers flair in open play.

Diego Gomez has history for scoring stunners by the way 🤯 The Brighton forward scored this in the @Carabao_Cup last year ⚽️ https://t.co/beBoDK8Rk8

While Brighton’s second goal owed to individual brilliance, their third was a sumptuous team strike. Charalampos Kostoulas’s back-heel on the right-hand side set up Yasin Ayari to tuck home. Dropping back and then running over the top, Kostoulas was a constant menace, fully deserving his goal in the 49th minute, when Ayari’s deflected shot fell into his path. Aged 19, Kostoulas is shaping up as Brighton’s next great discovery.

Only once has an M23 derby been more one-sided, when Palace thrashed Brighton 6-0 in 1950. The refrain of Brighton’s exultant fans on the train home – “Who put the ball in the Palace net? Half the f---ing team did” – will, you suspect, become a staple at the Amex.

Celebrating an unforgettable win! 😮‍💨👏 https://t.co/jkrY0ubdkQ

Calvert-Lewin cancels out Mbeumo’s opener as the points are shared at Elland Road. It is to be seen whether the result relieves pressure from Carrick’s shoulders. United are 14th in the league while Leeds move into the top seven.

Brighton now face the unusual task of playing five consecutive away matches against some tough opponents.

It’s all over at the Vitality. Rose finally gets his first Premier League win as Bournemouth head coach having gone maddeningly close in previous matches. Goals from Tavernier and Evanilson, and a Danso red card, decide this one.

A superb performance 👏 https://t.co/MucWlTrgTY

And that’s that. Brighton were outstanding and here they recorded their biggest-ever win over rivals Crystal Palace after blitzing three goals in the first 10 minutes of the match. Hurzeler’s side are up to second in the league, for now, and have won six matches in a row.

"Would you look at that!" DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 https://t.co/qmagVbGEb4

Hurzeler said before this afternoon’s match that he wanted Brighton to be “ruthless” and here we are: Brighton are 5-0 up in the 92nd minute and still they want more.

De Cuyper bursts into the box, attacking the left half-space, and wins yet another Brighton corner. Yalcouye goes short again, but his eventual cross is easily gathered by Benitez.

Brighton are content to keep the ball here as the clock winds down. Passes across the backline prompt oles from the crowd, but with Palace sitting off, Hadjam senses an opening and bursts down the left, earning a corner for  his troubles.

Yalcouye plays short and the ball is worked to Hadjam on the edge of the box, but his searching ball goalwards is not up to much.

There will be four minutes of time added on.

“We want six,” sing the Brighton fans as Rutter earns another corner. It’s the same inswinging delivery that is played to the far post, this time it is Dunk who gets there, but his header across goal is cleared on this occasion.

And it’s the former who gets away from his marker Hughes to head goalwards off the inswinging delivery, and while Benitez keeps the defender’s effort out, Hinshelwood is there to finish from a yard out.

Jack Hinshelwood adds another for Brighton! 🔵 https://t.co/vpvAVURe0i

Sage makes his fifth and final substitution with Kamada making way for Hughes.

Boscagli and Ayari’s excellent afternoons are over as Hadjam and Yalcouye enter the field of play in their place.

Wharton tries to thread an ambitious ball over the top for Mateta to run on to, but it gets away from the Frenchman and Verbruggen gathers with ease.

There have been so many stand-out performances from players in blue and white, but how good as Vuskovic been this afternoon? Did not give Strand Larsen a sniff, made 11 defensive contributions and has progressed the ball whenever required.

Ayari tiptoes in off the left side, chopping inside Richards into a dangerous position, but the ball gets away from him and he’s unable to get a shot away before the chance disappears.

Chance! Palace come close to a consolation goal, Lerma rising highest at a corner but his header grazes the outside of the post and out for a goal-kick.

Nketiah fails to square to Mateta in front of Brighton’s goal moments later, but it is immaterial as he was offside anyhow.

Hurzeler makes his first substitutions of the match. Rutter and Hinshelwood, both of whom scored in midweek, are on in place of Kostoulas and Gross.

Lerma makes a meal out of a routine clearance, inadvertently tapping the ball with his left foot on to his right and out for a corner, much to the delight of the Brighton fans. Gross sends the ball in but puts too much on his delivery and it sails over everyone.

Canvot comes through the back of Kostoulas inside Palace’s half and gives away a foul. The free-kick is flighted into the box but Palace clear their lines on this occasion.

There seems to be a bit of needle emerging on the touchline as Crystal Palace coach Paddy McCarthy berates Brighton’s bench. He receives a yellow card for his troubles. Arguably the most intensity we’ve seen from the visitors all match.

Well that sums up Palace’s afternoon perfectly. It’s a terrible miss by Mateta, who has only just come on.

Nketiah combines nicely with McNeil in the left half-space before picking out the Frenchman in space inside the box, but his left-footed effort balloons on to the crossbar from a seemingly unmissable position. So, so poor.

More changes for Palace. Pino and Strand Larsen make way for Nketiah and Mateta.

One triumph of Brighton’s counter-pressing system is that they seemingly create “plus-one” situations across the entirety of the pitch. This cannot be the case, of course, but in the time it takes for Palace’s creators to pick out spaces, a Brighton marker is already on to them.

Lerma has replaced Ahanor as Sage looks to stem the tide. Brighton refuse to remove their foot from the pedal, though, and Gross spins in another free-kick, which is cleared, but only to Vuskovic on the edge of the box. The defender attempts to shape the ball into the top corner but makes too true of a contact and it sails well over.

Brighton have scored at least three goals in eight of their 11 matches this season.

51 - Diego Gómez's goal for Brighton against Crystal Palace was from 51 metres, the furthest range Premier League goal since Wayne Rooney for Everton v West Ham in November 2017 (58m). Incredible. https://t.co/Xm4lH1FLH7

Absolute domination. Muffled boos are heard from the away end as the referee brings the first half to a close. The Palace fans are still reeling after watching their side concede three times in the opening 10 minutes.

It’s really been a case of asphyxiation by counter-press for Palace here. Brighton have pounced on every loose touch and when they regain possession their forward players burst forth with further runners supporting underneath. It’s what they have been doing all season, but stopping it - even when you know it’s coming - is no easy feat.

There will be two minutes of time added on at the end of the first half.

It’s remarkable how easily Brighton are finding space between the lines, they’re pulling Palace’s markers to and fro, into and out of position.

Richards does get another go at tossing another throw-in back into the box, this time from the right, and Khalaili gets to this one, but heads well over.

Brighton utterly in control. They are dominating the ball and playing in a very controlled way, then bursting into life when Palace advance themselves.

Gomez has been fantastic this afternoon and he tiptoes his way past several Palace midfielders along the halfway line. Boscagli then has the presence of mind to switch the ball back out to the right and Gross’ set into the path of Kadioglu is struck goalwards and tipped behind by Benitez.

For the first time this afternoon, Mitchell makes a meaningful foray forward. He earns a throw-in near the corner flag which Richards launches into the box, but the ball slips out of his hands and Brighton clear their lines.

The resulting corner lands to Gross off the second phase but he cannot keep his effort down. He spins on his heels in frustration.

The hosts are letting Palace have the ball, settling into their defensive structure and funnelling the visitors around the outside, using the touchline as an extra defender to force errors.

Kadiologu works the ball infield from the right but cannot pick out Kostoulas. De Cuyper works the ball back into the middle for Ayari to strike goalwards from just outside the box, his effort takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner.

It’s taken Gross 30 minutes to make his first misstep. He goes into the book for a desperate tackle on Pino who had taken the ball away from the German with a superb first touch.

Close! A raking crossfield pass to Gomez at the far post is put back across the face of goal and a prone Ahanor is just about able to clear his lines. The young defender knew very little about that.

Brighton have complete control of the central areas, with Wharton and Timber struggling to get on top of their web of rotations and diversionary runs.

Palace win a free-kick 25 yards out and Pino, who has two goals in his last two outings, tries his luck but cannot clear the wall.

Brighton waste no time getting up the pitch and Kostoulas has a go from outside the box. His effort is straight at Benitez who gathers the ball at the second time of asking.

Danso is shown a red card as things go bad to worse for Sunderland at the Vitality. He brought down Evanilson as the Brazilian looked to be through on goal.

Finally some respite for Palace as Brighton choose to circulate the ball in front of their first line of pressure.

But back come the hosts soon after, De Cuyper bursting into the left of the box. This time Benitez is wise to the move and gets out smartly to cut it out.

Chants of “Are you Arsenal in disguise” ring out around the Amex...

This is utterly surreal. Gómez’s incredible strike had barely sunk in when Brighton harassed Palace again. This was a sumptuous team strike: a back heel from Kostoulas on the right setting up Ayari to tuck home. The atmosphere at Amex is electric. Brighton are heading second, below only Manchester City.

Brighton 3 Crystal Palace 0 (Gomez) Wow. Brighton are in dreamland here. Kostoulas finds space down the right and picks out the onrushing Ayari, whose effort beats Benitez via a Canvot deflection. That’s three goals in the first 10 minutes.

"Crystal Palace blown away here!" Brighton score a THIRD inside 10 minutes 🔥 https://t.co/YyoIw1zyaJ

Brighton 2 Crystal Palace 0 (Gomez) My goodness... That’s a goal-of-the-season contender, surely?! Wharton cedes possession on the halfway line and Gomez does the rest. He’s at most a yard inside Palace’s half and, spotting Benitez off his line, tries his luck from distance and finds the back of the net!

Goal of the season? From the halfway line, Diego Gómez picks up a loose ball and lobs Walter Benítez: shades of David Beckham at Wimbledon 30 years ago. Palace are in disarray.

"Would you look at that!" DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 https://t.co/qmagVbGEb4

Brighton only need three-and-a-half minutes to get their opener: a Pascal Gross free-kick from the left-hand side, headed into his own net by Palace centre-half Jaydee Canvot. Just the tonic for the thousands of Brighton fans being soaked.

Jaydee Canvot glances the ball into his own net and Brighton lead! 🔵 https://t.co/subm9ggwId

Kadioglu sets the tone early on, snapping in to cut off a loose pass out from the back by Palace. The ball is eventually worked up to Kostoulas, but he cannot bring it under his spell.

The heavens have opened up at the Amex, but that has not dampened the stadium announcer’s enthusiasm. He announces each player to the fans, with Pascal “the Goat” Gross’ name receiving an especially hearty cheer from the crowd.

The players (all 22 starters, it seems) take a knee before Brighton get us started.

The clouds have come in and the rain has started at the Amex as kick-off approaches. A raucous atmosphere, as you’d expect for the M23 derby, with plenty of Brighton fans relishing singing anti-Crystal Palace songs on the way to the ground. Should Brighton win - as they will expect to - they will move second, at least until Arsenal play later.

Kick-off is almost upon us. There’s just about enough time to make a brew before the action begins...

Eighteen-year-old defender Honest Ahanor starts in Palace’s back three alongside Jaydee Canvot, 20, and Chris Richards, 26. This afternoon will be a decent examination of their credentials as a unit. The Italy defender is on loan from Atalanta and will join Chelsea next summer.

The police-to-fan ratio looks fairly healthy here...

Palace fans head to #Brighton Station more on @brightonargus https://t.co/LQ9MKobmFH

Brighton’s form is all the more impressive given that Hurzeler has not had recourse to key men in Yankuba Minteh, Kaoru Mitoma and Mats Wieffer.

Femi Azeez, signed from Millwall in the summer for £15m, has only featured in a friendly match during the international break and remains sidelined with a muscle issue.

These missing men are nearing returns, and it makes you wonder whether Brighton can reach even further heights.

There will be supporters of both sides who are not particularly moved by this match-up. Some Crystal Palace fans may argue that their rivalry with Nottingham Forest has been more intense in recent years.

When asked about the rivalry, Sage said: “I know that the fans don’t like this name [the M23 derby] because it is too far to name it this. We know it is a big game for the club and the fans, and we have to show our better phases, like the second halves of our last two games.”

Interestingly, the categories in which Brighton have excelled marry up almost perfectly with Crystal Palace’s weakest areas. Here are their numbers in the same/reciprocal departments:

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

#1410. Merseyside Derby & Two More January Fixtures Moved For Live Broadcast

Three of Everton's Premier League fixtures in January – including the Merseyside derby at Anfield – have been moved for live television coverage.

The Toffees' trip to Coventry City remains on Saturday 16 January, but with an earlier kick-off time of 12.30pm (GMT), and will be shown live on TNT Sports.

The following weekend, David Moyes' side will now host Brentford at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday 24 January, in a 2pm (GMT) kick-off that will be broadcast live on Sky Sports.

#1409. Leicester City AXE controversial deal with unlicensed gambling company after sponsor sparked fan fury by appointing 'international porn star' as ambassador

Published: 14:09 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EST, 18 November 2026

Leicester have decided to end their deal with controversial sponsors BC.GAME six months ahead of schedule.

Fans expressed fury and dismay earlier this month after the club's unlicensed gambling shirt sponsor appointed an 'international porn star' as its new ambassador.

Now Leicester have opted to conclude the partnership – in a move welcomed by supporters. A statement on Wednesday read: ‘The decision follows constructive discussions between both parties in recent days, during which we recognised our differing commercial priorities moving forward.

‘We would like to thank BC.GAME for its support throughout its two-and-a-half-year association with Leicester City and for the constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement.

‘Supporters who have purchased a BC.GAME-branded replica shirt through official LCFC retail channels within the last 28 days (since 21 October, 2026) can return it for a full refund or exchange (subject to availability) by Wednesday 2 December.’

BC.GAME, an online casino company, had been the Foxes' primary shirt sponsor since the start of the 2024-25 season. They announced a partnership with Russian adult content creator Eva Elfie in a video on X earlier this month.

Leicester City have axed a partnership with BC.GAME, after the gambling shirt sponsor appointed 'international porn star' Eva Elfie as its new ambassador

Leicester confirmed fans who have purchased a replica shirt featuring the sponsor's name within the last 28 days can return it for a full refund or exchange by December 2

Elfie, who has 4.8million Instagram followers, is known in Esports and gaming communities too

In recent years, Leicester’s spectacular decline on the pitch has mirrored the relationship with their supporters.

During the years immediately before and after their stunning Premier League triumph in 2016, it was difficult to find a club more in tune with the fanbase.

But a series of baffling decisions – including the tie-up with BC.GAME – eroded trust between the club and their supporters.

Leicester are now in League One and face a long road back but sensible moves like this one suggest they are at least facing in the right direction again.

#1407. Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers1,2,3,4,8,9. Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8+ T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies10,11,12,13. However, ferroptotic cells limit this response8,9,10,14, resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE2 production or disrupting PGE2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

Uncontrolled lipid peroxidation is integral to ferroptosis5,15. Cancer cells are commonly protected from unrestrained lipid peroxidation and spontaneous ferroptotic cell death by molecular defence systems such as the system xc––glutathione (GSH)–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) pathway5,16, in which GPX4 is the key enzyme mediating lipid peroxide detoxification. Strategies to promote ferroptosis by blockade of ferroptosis defence systems, such as GPX4 inhibitors, have been considered promising approaches to achieve tumour elimination in patients with difficult-to-treat cancers8,9. Studies using preclinical mouse models have uncovered that effective tumour elimination by ferroptosis-inducing strategies requires anticancer immunity by DCs10 and tumour-infiltrating CD8+ T cells11,12,13. Yet recent findings have suggested that DC-driven anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity is suppressed in ferroptotic tumours8,9,10,17. Emerging evidence has implicated that the unrestrained generation of membrane lipid peroxides in ferroptotic cells can promote the production and release of molecules that may impact immune cell functions18. However, what causes the suppression of DC-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity in the context of tumour ferroptosis remains largely unclear.

Potentially relevant immunoregulatory factors produced by ferroptotic cancer cells are oxylipins, bioactive lipids generated through peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane lipids, a hallmark of ferroptosis15. To assess ferroptosis-induced oxylipin production and identify key factors, we profiled the oxylipin secretome of mouse BRAF(V600E) and NRAS(G12D) melanoma, 4T1 breast cancer and MC38 colorectal cancer cells following RSL3-induced ferroptosis. Across all these cancer cell lines, RSL3-treated (ferroptotic) cells displayed increased production of oxylipins compared with untreated (non-ferroptotic) controls (Fig. 1a). Of note, in all groups, the eicosanoid PGE2 was by far the most abundant oxylipin upregulated by ferroptosis induction (Fig. 1a). Similar to ferroptosis induction by RSL3 (which inhibits selenoproteins beyond GPX4), we observed strong PGE2 production after genetic ablation of the ferroptosis-protective enzyme GPX4, ferroptosis induction using the GPX4 inhibitor ML210 or erastin-mediated inactivation of system xc–-mediated cystine import (Extended Data Fig. 1a–f). Thus, ferroptosis may trigger the production of PGE2 in cancer cells, which is a notable finding given the important role of PGE2 for suppression of anticancer immunity19,20,21.

a, Oxylipin profiles for the indicated cancer cell lines after RSL3 treatment. 4-HDHA, 4-hydroxydocosahexaenoic acid; 5,6-DHET, 5,6-dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acid; 6R-LXA4, 6R-lipoxin A4; 11-HETE, 11-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid; 15-oxoETE, 15-oxoeicosatetraenoic acid; DMSO, dimethyl sulfoxide; PDX, protectin DX; RvD1, resolvin D1; vs, versus. The vertical dotted line indicates a fold change (FC) (log2) of 0. b, PGE2 production by cancer cell lines after induction of ferroptosis, immunogenic cell death (ICD) or apoptosis. n = 4 samples for BRAF(V600E) melanoma, and n = 3 samples for NRAS(G12D) melanoma, 4T1 breast cancer and MC38 colorectal cancer. NS, not significant. c–f, Functional analyses of cDC1s exposed to dying cancer cell conditioned medium (CM). Experimental design (c). CXCL9 production by cDC1s; the plots show one cDC1 culture representative of n = 4 cultures (d). Quantification of CXCL9+ cDC1s, based on panel d; n = 4 samples (e). Analysis of cDC1s by RNA-seq (n = 4); the volcano plots show the effect of CM from ferroptotic (left) or apoptotic (right) BRAF(V600E) cells on activation-induced cDC1 genes (f). PE, phycoerythrin; RNA-seq, RNA sequencing; SSC-A, side scatter area. Data show mean ± s.e.m. of n = 3 biological replicates (a). In b, the centre line indicates the mean and the bounds show the minimum and maximum values. In e, the centre line indicates the median, the bounds extend from the 25th to the 75th percentile, and the whiskers correspond to he minimum and maximum values. P values are from one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (two-sided; b,e). Differentially expressed genes were identified using a two-sided Wald test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (f).

By contrast, stimulation of ultraviolet B (UVB)-induced apoptosis, doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death or necrocide 1 (NC1)-induced necrotic cell death failed to promote PGE2 production (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1g). However, PGE2 production was induced in cells undergoing necroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 1h). These findings imply that PGE2 production is selectively induced by as yet unknown molecular events in ferroptotic cells and that these events, at least to some extent, may be shared with necroptotic cells.

Using liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1), we further validated that ferroptotic cancer cells depend on lipid peroxides to produce PGE2 (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This was not the case for key effectors of other cell death pathways, such as caspases or receptor-interacting serine–threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1; Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We extended our analyses to a broader panel of mouse and human cancer cells, including established cell lines, cells from spontaneous mouse cancer models and cells from patients with pancreatic cancer. In all these cells, RSL3-induced ferroptosis triggered markedly increased PGE2 production (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Together, these data suggest that ferroptosis promotes aberrant production of PGE2 in mouse and human cancer cells, prompting us to investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms and consequences for anticancer immunity.

Effective anticancer immunity often depends on cDC1s22,23, which fulfil essential roles in the priming of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses24,25 and effector differentiation and expansion of CD8+ tumour-infiltrating T lymphocytes (TILs)26,27. These cDC1 functions are impacted by immunoregulatory factors derived from dying cancer cells22,23,28; however, how mediators released by ferroptotic cancer cells impact cDC1s and their functions is not known.

To address this issue, we generated cDC1s from bone marrow cells, exposed them to conditioned medium from RSL3-induced, ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells and assessed their functional properties after activation with polyinosinic–polycytidylic acid (poly(I:C); Fig. 1c). The conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells strongly compromised the capacity of cDC1s to produce CXCL9 (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a), a chemokine required for cDC1-mediated orchestration of CD8+ TIL responses26,29. Similar results were observed for cDC1 production of the T cell stimulatory cytokine interleukin-12 (IL-12)30 (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). By contrast, no impairment was observed for cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from cancer cells undergoing apoptosis or doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Impaired CXCL9 production was similarly observed for splenic cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells (Extended Data Fig. 3d). These results suggest that factors released by ferroptotic cancer cells disable cDC1s from producing molecules required to promote anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity.

cDC1 functions are controlled by transcriptional programming31,32. We therefore subjected cDC1s activated by poly(I:C) following exposure to ferroptotic or apoptotic BRAF(V600E) cell conditioned medium to transcriptional profiling by RNA sequencing. We found that ferroptotic, but not apoptotic, cancer cell-derived factors induced prominent transcriptional changes in cDC1s (Fig. 1f), including impaired expression of genes encoding stimulatory cytokines (including Ifnb and Ifnl2), T cell-recruiting chemokines (Cxcl9 and Ccl4) and integrins important for T cell activation (Itgal; Fig. 1f). We also confirmed the inhibitory effect on cDC1 cytokine and chemokine production at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Of note, we did not detect a defect in upregulation of MHC or costimulatory molecules (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 1), implying that ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors do not prevent cDC1 activation. Of note, many of the genes impaired in cDC1s following exposure to ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors were shared with a core gene set of PGE2-mediated cDC1 dysfunction (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g and Supplementary Table 1), although genes beyond this set were also impaired. Consistently, gene set enrichment analyses revealed a prominent impairment of PGE2-regulated functional cDC1 genes (Extended Data Fig. 3h), whereas genes associated with migration or antigen processing (that is, molecular programs not regulated by PGE2 signalling in cDC1s19), remained unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 3h). Together, these data suggest that ferroptotic cancer cells promote cDC1 dysfunction and that this is mediated by PGE2.

Similar to cancer cells, ferroptosis induction caused aberrant PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a), an established mouse embryonic fibroblast model often used to study the molecular underpinnings of ferroptosis33. This was linked to markedly increased transcript and protein expression of the key PGE2-producing enzyme COX2 (encoded by Ptgs2; Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). Lip-1 treatment rescued this effect (Fig. 2a), whereas stimulation of lipid peroxidation by cumene hydroperoxide promoted both Ptgs2 expression and increased PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). Together, these results point towards a requirement of membrane lipid peroxide generation for PGE2 production through transcriptional regulation of COX2. Using COX inhibitors, we also confirmed that COX activity was required for PGE2 production by ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2b), but dispensable for execution of ferroptotic cell death (Fig. 2c).

a–r, Molecular analyses of RSL3-induced, ferroptotic Pfa1 cells. Transcript expression of COX–PGE2 pathway enzymes; n = 3 samples (a). mPtges1, microsomal Ptges1. Effect of CXB (1, 10 or 100 nM) or acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) (1, 10 or 100 µM) on PGE2 production (b) and cell viability (c); n = 3 samples. Microscopy analysis of Ca2+ influx (fluo-8-AM) after 8 h (d). Scale bars, 10 µm. The dashed lines indicate cell borders. Quantification of Ca2+ influx, based on panel d; n = 45 cells for DMSO control and n = 60 cells for RSL3 (e). Time-resolved live cell imaging of lipid peroxidation (BODIPY C11), Ca2+ influx (CalBryte 630-AM) and cell death (Sytox blue); n = 4 samples (f). Effect of PEG treatment; n = 3 samples (g–j): experimental design (g); quantification of Ptgs2 mRNA (h) and COX2 protein (i) expression after 8 h; and measurement of PGE2 production (j). Effect of EGTA on PGE2 production; n = 3 samples (k). Representative western blot of p-p38 protein expression after 8 h (l). Quantification of p-p38 and total p38 expression, based on panel l; n = 3 samples (m). Effect of SB203580-mediated p38 MAPK inhibition on COX2 expression after 8 h (n), PGE2 production (o) and cell viability (p); n = 3 samples. Effect of Lip-1 on cell viability (q). Oxylipin profiles of cells treated as indicated; n = 3 samples (r). DHETE, dihydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid; DiHOME, dihydroxyoctadecenoic acid; EET, epoxyeicosatrienoic acid; EpOME, epoxy octadecenoic acid; HETrE, hydroxyeicosatrienoic acid; HODE, hydroxyoctadecadienoic acid; LOOH, lipid hydroperoxide; TXB2, thromboxane B2. s, Schematic illustrating the mechanistic underpinnings of PGE2 production in ferroptotic cancer cells. Data depict mean ± s.e.m. (b,c,p,q). Data are depicted as boxplots (h–k,m–o). Plots show data for one sample of n = 6 samples from two independent experiments (d,f,l). In h–k,m–o, the centre line indicates the mean and the bounds show the minimum and maximum values. P values are from one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (b,c,h–k,m–q) or unpaired Student’s t-tests (e). NS (P ≥ 0.05).

A key event caused by lipid peroxides in ferroptotic cells is the influx of extracellular Ca2+ (ref. 5), which constitutes an early event in pro-ferroptotic cells before the onset of cell death. Consistently, microscopy imaging revealed high intracellular Ca2+ levels in Pfa1 cells early after RSL3-mediated ferroptosis induction (Fig. 2d,e), which was similarly observed for multiple mouse cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). Time-resolved live cell imaging of ferroptotic Pfa1 cells confirmed that Ca2+ influx followed peroxide accumulation, but occurred before the cell death-associated loss of plasma membrane integrity (Fig. 2f). Of note, preventing Ca2+ influx through polyethylene glycol (PEG)-mediated blockade of membrane permeabilization-enabled osmotic molecule exchange5,34,35 (Fig. 2g and Extended Data Fig. 4i,j) abrogated the upregulation of Ptgs2 mRNA (Fig. 2h) and COX2 protein expression (Fig. 2i) in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells, resulting in a loss of PGE2 production (Fig. 2j). We also validated that lipid peroxide generation was only minimally affected by PEG treatment (Extended Data Fig. 4k,l) and that ferroptotic cells become permeable to other small extracellular molecules5, including sodium ions (Na+; Extended Data Fig. 4m–p).

Gain-of-function experiments using ionomycin, which selectively transport extracellular Ca2+ into cells, revealed that Ca2+ influx alone was sufficient to promote COX2 upregulation and PGE2 production across Pfa1, BRAF(V600E) melanoma and MC38 colorectal cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 4q,r). Thus, although small molecules beyond Ca2+ enter ferroptotic cells, they probably do not contribute substantially to the activation of COX-mediated PGE2 production. Consistently, blockade of Ca2+ influx using the Ca2+ chelator EGTA confirmed the relevance of Ca2+ signalling for PGE2 production in ferroptotic cells (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 4s,t).

Ca2+ influx can regulate gene expression via p38 MAPK signalling, which requires p38 MAPK activatory phosphorylation (p-p38). Consistently, ferroptotic Pfa1 cells displayed a prominent increase in p-p38 levels (Fig. 2l,m), which was abolished by PEG treatment (Fig. 2l,m). Moreover, treatment with the selective p38 MAPK inhibitor SB203580 abrogated the upregulation of COX2 expression and PGE2 production in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2n,o), demonstrating the relevance of p38 MAPK signalling for PGE2 production. Of note, the later execution of cell death remained unaffected by p38 MAPK inhibition (Fig. 2p) or blockade of Ca2+ influx (Extended Data Fig. 5a). These results suggest that Ca2+-induced p38 MAPK signalling is not required for ferroptotic cell death. We also confirmed that SB203580 did not induce cell death in non-ferroptotic cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a), and that the death of SB203580-treated ferroptotic Pfa1 cells was rescued by Lip-1 (Fig. 2q).

Oxylipin profiling revealed a selective requirement of p38 MAPK signalling for production of PGE2 and other COX-derived eicosanoids in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2r), whereas other oxylipins remained largely unaffected. Similar to Pfa1 cells, PEG-mediated inhibition of Ca2+ influx or inhibition of p38 MAPK abolished PGE2 production in ferroptotic cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 5b–e), demonstrating the relevance of Ca2+-mediated p38 MAPK pathway activation for PGE2 production also in ferroptotic cancer cells. We also confirmed that, in cancer cells, this mechanistic axis is already active in the early phase after ferroptosis induction (Extended Data Fig. 5f–r) and that p38 MAPK signalling is dispensable for the propagation of ferroptotic cell death (Extended Data Fig. 5s–v). Experiments with cells deficient in p38α (the p38 MAPK isoform commonly expressed in cancer cells) further validated that p38 MAPK signalling is required for PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 5w,x), but not their cell death execution (Extended Data Fig. 5y). We conclude that Ca2+-mediated activation of p38 MAPK signalling triggers PGE2 production by ferroptotic cells and that this mechanism is not required for ferroptosis-dependent cancer cell death (Fig. 2s). This molecular uncoupling enables to selectively interfere with p38 MAPK pathway activity to impair PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells while preserving ferroptosis-mediated cancer cell elimination.

To test whether ferroptotic cancer cells depend on PGE2 to promote cDC1 dysfunction, we induced ferroptosis in COX-deficient Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells, which cannot produce PGE2 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c). We then exposed cDC1s to conditioned medium from ferroptotic Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− or control BRAF(V600E) cells, activated them by poly(I:C) and compared their gene expression profile by RNA sequencing (Fig. 3a). We also included cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from apoptotic BRAF(V600E) cells, to test possible effects of dying cancer cell-derived factors unrelated to ferroptosis. We observed that PGE2 deficiency in ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells prevented cDC1 reprogramming (Fig. 3b) and, consequently, rescued the expression of functional cDC1 genes (for example, Irf8, Ifnl2 and Cxcl9; Fig. 3c). This regain of gene expression was similarly observed in a more detailed analysis of the core functional cDC1 genes selectively suppressed by factors from ferroptotic, but not apoptotic, BRAF(V600E) cells (Fig. 3d).

a, Experimental design for panels b–d. b, Principal component (PC) analysis of differentially expressed genes in cDC1s treated as indicated. c, Effect of COX deficiency in ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells on gene expression of poly(I:C)-activated cDC1. d, Heatmap showing the expression of core functional cDC1 genes. e–g, Effect of EP2/EP4 deficiency on ferroptotic cancer cell-induced cDC1 dysfunction: heatmap showing the expression of core functional genes in WT or ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl cDC1s treated as indicated (e); flow cytometry plots showing CXCL9 expression, with one of n = 5 samples (f); and quantification of CXCL9+ cDC1s, based on panel f (g; n = 6 samples for WT, and n = 5 samples for ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl). Data show mean ± s.e.m. h,i, Effect of ferroptotic cancer cell-derived CM on cDC1-induced CD8+ T cell expansion: experimental design (h), and quantification of CD8+ T cell expansion (i; n = 3 samples). In i, the centre line indicates the mean and the bounds show the minimum and maximum values. Differentially expressed genes were identified by two-sided Wald test with multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg method (c). P values are from one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (g,i). NS (P ≥ 0.05).

The inhibitory effect of PGE2 on immune cells36, including cDC1s19, is mediated by signalling through the PGE2 receptors EP2 (encoded by Ptger2) and EP4 (encoded by Ptger4). We therefore extended our RNA sequencing analyses to EP2/EP4-deficient cDC1s from ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice19,26. Whereas conditioned medium from PGE2-producing ferroptotic control BRAF(V600E) cells compromised the upregulation of activation induced genes in (EP2/EP4-proficient) wildtype (WT) cDC1s, this defect was fully rescued in EP2/EP4-deficient cDC1s (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Table 2). This result demonstrates the relevance of PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling for ferroptotic cancer cell-mediated impairment of cDC1 functions. In separate experiments, we further validated that CXCL9 and IL-12 production is rescued in both EP2/EP4-deficient cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells and cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from (PGE2-deficient) ferroptotic Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− (BRAF(V600E)) cells (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 6d,e). Using CXCL9 as a functional marker, we also confirmed that PGE2 was similarly required for ferroptotic cancer cell-mediated inhibition of cDC1s activated by stimuli reported to promote cDC1 activation in tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6f,g). In a T cell stimulation assay, we further probed the ability of cDC1s to stimulate CD8+ T cell expansion. This function was similarly rescued in cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from PGE2-deficient ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells (Fig. 3h,i). Using celecoxib (CXB)-mediated blockade of PGE2 production, we also confirmed that other ferroptotic cancer cells depend on PGE2 to inhibit cDC1 function, as determined by CXCL9 staining (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i). Together, these findings suggest that PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling mediates the impairment of cDC1 functions caused by ferroptotic cancer cells. Moreover, EP2/EP4 deficiency rescues cDC1s from ferroptotic cancer cell-mediated inhibition.

Our results raised the question whether cDC1s can mount effective CD8+ T cell responses against ferroptotic cancer cells when protected from inhibitory PGE2 signalling. To address this issue, we adoptively transferred CD8+ OT-I T cells, which express a transgenic T cell receptor (TCR) specific for the model antigen ovalbumin (OVA), into WT mice subsequently transplanted with ferroptotic, OVA-expressing control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) cells (Extended Data Fig. 7a). To determine the relevance of EP2/EP4-mediated PGE2 signalling in cDC1, we further included Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, which lack EP2 and EP4 in CLEC9A-expressing cDC1. Analyses of OT-I T cell expansion in lymphoid tissues revealed that ferroptotic cancer cell-derived PGE2 impairs the productive generation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses through PGE2-mediated inhibition of cDC1 functions (Extended Data Fig. 7b–e). Moreover, OT-I T cell expansion was lost in cDC1-deficient Batf3−/− mice challenged with ferroptotic BRAF(V600E)–OVA cells (Extended Data Fig. 7f), confirming the functional relevance of cDC1s for generation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses.

To determine whether ferroptotic tumours depend on PGE2 production to restrict cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8+ TIL responses and escape immune control, we analysed the growth of (ferroptotic) Gpx4−/− or (non-ferroptotic) WT MC38 cells transplanted into WT and Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Fig. 4a). By microscopy-based analysis of the ferroptosis marker 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) and COX2 protein, we confirmed cancer cell ferroptosis leading to enhanced COX pathway activity in Gpx4−/−, but not WT, MC38 tumours (Extended Data Fig. 8). In WT mice, tumours formed by Gpx4−/− MC38 cells exhibited progressive tumour growth, which was only minimally slower than WT MC38 cells (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9a). These data are consistent with inefficient control of ferroptotic cancers in immunocompetent mice. By contrast, Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice exhibited improved tumour immune control and fully rejected Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9a). By contrast, WT MC38 tumours displayed reduced growth but failed to be eliminated in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9a). Of note, this pattern was similarly observed for Cd4crePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice in which T cells lack EP2/EP4 expression (Extended Data Fig. 9b), implying that ferroptotic tumours, in parallel to inhibiting cDC1, depend on PGE2-mediated inhibition of T cells to escape anticancer immunity.
